narration: <bookmark mark='bits'/>A stick measured in small units has many pieces.
In a big unit, the same stick has few.
<bookmark mark='mult'/>When we change to a smaller unit, the number gets bigger, so we multiply.
<bookmark mark='div'/>When we change to a bigger unit, the number gets smaller, so we divide.
beats.on_screen: a long stick cut into small bits: smaller unit, bigger number, multiply; bigger unit, smaller number, divide

marks.given: the unit facts and the six measures are written in the working band

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the unit facts, and six measures to change into a new unit.

marks.find: the find line is written under the given line

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find each measure in the new unit.
beats.on_screen: To find: each measure in the new unit

marks.why: the step title and the three measures that go to a smaller unit are lit

narration: <bookmark mark='why'/>Step one, three measures go to a smaller unit, so we multiply.
<bookmark mark='km'/>Five point five kilometres: one kilometre is one thousand metres.
Multiply five point five by one thousand.
<bookmark mark='cm'/>Fourteen point five centimetres: one centimetre is ten millimetres.
Multiply fourteen point five by ten.
<bookmark mark='m'/>Nine point zero two metres: one metre is one hundred centimetres, and each centimetre is ten millimetres.
<bookmark mark='mm'/>That makes one metre one thousand millimetres, so we multiply by one thousand.
beats.on_screen: Step 1, to a smaller unit, multiply: 5.5 km to m: 5.5 × 1000; 14.5 cm to mm: 14.5 × 10; 9.02 m to mm: 1 m = 100 cm = 100 × 10 mm = 1000 mm, so 9.02 × 1000

marks.why: the step title and the three measures that go to a bigger unit are lit

narration: <bookmark mark='why'/>Step two, three measures go to a bigger unit, so we divide.
<bookmark mark='cm'/>Thirty five centimetres: one metre is one hundred centimetres.
Divide thirty five by one hundred.
<bookmark mark='g'/>Sixty eight grams: one kilogram is one thousand grams.
Divide sixty eight by one thousand.
<bookmark mark='ml'/>One hundred twenty five point five millilitres: one litre is one thousand millilitres.
Divide by one thousand.
beats.on_screen: Step 2, to a bigger unit, divide: 35 cm to m: 35 ÷ 100; 68 g to kg: 68 ÷ 1000; 125.5 ml to l: 125.5 ÷ 1000

marks.left: ÷ 100 and ÷ 1000 are written with arrows to the left of two places and three places
marks.zero: a zero fills an empty place
marks.right: × 10 and × 1000 are written with arrows to the right of one place and three places

narration: <bookmark mark='right'/>Step three, multiplying moves the decimal point to the right.
Ten moves it one place, and one thousand moves it three places.
<bookmark mark='left'/>Dividing moves the decimal point to the left.
One hundred moves it two places, and one thousand moves it three places.
<bookmark mark='zero'/>We fill any empty place with a zero.
beats.on_screen: Step 3: × 10: point 1 place right; × 1000: point 3 places right; ÷ 100: point 2 places left; ÷ 1000: point 3 places left; empty places get zeros

marks.cmp: each result is compared with its starting number
marks.rule: the check words are written: bigger unit, smaller number; smaller unit, bigger number

narration: <bookmark mark='cmp'/>Step four, check each result against the number we began with.
<bookmark mark='rule'/>Going from kilometres to metres, the number must grow.
Going from centimetres to metres, the number must shrink.
beats.on_screen: Step 4: check the size: a bigger unit gives a smaller number; a smaller unit gives a bigger number

marks.ans: the six blanks are filled and boxed

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Each blank is filled by multiplying or dividing by ten, a hundred or a thousand.
<bookmark mark='pair1'/>Five point five kilometres is five thousand five hundred metres.
Thirty five centimetres is zero point three five metres.
<bookmark mark='pair2'/>Fourteen point five centimetres is one hundred forty five millimetres.
Sixty eight grams is zero point zero six eight kilograms.
<bookmark mark='pair3'/>Nine point zero two metres is nine thousand twenty millimetres.
One hundred twenty five point five millilitres is zero point one two five five litres.

video_script.design: One idea: a smaller unit means a bigger number, so multiply; a bigger unit means a smaller number, so divide. The unit facts stay on the board all video; the working band shows the six operations in two steps, then the decimal point rule, and the answers appear only in the answer beat.
source: End of chapter Figure it Out, Q5
video_script.payoff_line: Each blank is filled by multiplying or dividing by ten, a hundred or a thousand

final_answer.spoken: five thousand five hundred metres, zero point three five metres, one hundred forty five millimetres, zero point zero six eight kilograms, nine thousand twenty millimetres and zero point one two five five litres

video_script.substitution: A smaller unit means multiplying by the number of small units in one big unit, and a bigger unit means dividing by it, which moves the decimal point.

media.teaching_notes: One idea: a smaller unit needs a bigger number, so multiply; a bigger unit needs a smaller number, so divide; and ten, a hundred or a thousand move the decimal point one, two or three places. Ask the class whether the number of metres should be bigger or smaller than the number of kilometres before any work is shown. Watch for students who multiply when they should divide.

content.text: One $210$ gram packet of peanut chikki costs ₹$70.5$, while a $110$ gram packet of potato chips costs ₹$33.25$. Which is cheaper?
content.question: A 210 gram packet of peanut chikki costs ₹70.5, while a 110 gram packet of potato chips costs ₹33.25. Which is cheaper?
content.question_tex: One $210$ gram packet of peanut chikki costs ₹$70.5$, while a $110$ gram packet of potato chips costs ₹$33.25$. Which is cheaper?
content.publication_text: One $210$ gram packet of peanut chikki costs ₹$70.5$, while a $110$ gram packet of potato chips costs ₹$33.25$. Which is cheaper?

content.text:
$1$. Chikki: $70.5 \div 210 = 0.3357$..., so about ₹$0.336$ per gram.
$2$. Chips: $33.25 \div 110 = 0.3022$..., so about ₹$0.302$ per gram.
$3$. $0.302 < 0.336$, so the potato chips are cheaper per gram.
Answer: The potato chips (about ₹$0.302$ per gram against about ₹$0.336$)
steps: Chikki: 70.5 ÷ 210 = 0.3357..., so about ₹0.336 per gram.
Chips: 33.25 ÷ 110 = 0.3022..., so about ₹0.302 per gram.
0.302 < 0.336, so the potato chips are cheaper per gram.

content.text: A teacher placed books that are $2.5\text{ cm}$ thick on a bookshelf. The teacher wanted to place $80$ books on the shelf. The bookshelf is $160\text{ cm}$ long. How many books could be placed on the shelf? Was there any space left? If yes, how much?
content.question: A teacher placed books that are 2.5 cm thick on a bookshelf. The teacher wanted to place 80 books on the shelf. The bookshelf is 160 cm long. How many books could be placed on the shelf? Was there any space left? If yes, how much?
content.question_tex: A teacher placed books that are $2.5\text{ cm}$ thick on a bookshelf. The teacher wanted to place $80$ books on the shelf. The bookshelf is $160\text{ cm}$ long. How many books could be placed on the shelf? Was there any space left? If yes, how much?
content.publication_text: A teacher placed books that are $2.5\text{ cm}$ thick on a bookshelf. The teacher wanted to place $80$ books on the shelf. The bookshelf is $160\text{ cm}$ long. How many books could be placed on the shelf? Was there any space left? If yes, how much?

content.text:
$1$. Books that fit: $160 \div 2.5 = 1600 \div 25 = 64$.
$2$. $64$ books take $64 \times 2.5 = 160\text{ cm}$, so no space is left.
$3$. $80$ books would need $80 \times 2.5 = 200\text{ cm}$, more than the shelf.
Answer: $64$ books; no space left, as $80$ books would need $200\text{ cm}$
steps: 64 books take 64 × 2.5 = 160 cm, so no space is left.
80 books would need 80 × 2.5 = 200 cm, more than the shelf.
content.answer: 64 books; no space left (80 books would need 200 cm)

narration: <bookmark mark='why'/>Step one, fifteen point six times one point two.
<bookmark mark='digits'/>The digits are the same as one hundred fifty six times twelve.
That is one thousand eight hundred seventy two.
<bookmark mark='count'/>Each number has one decimal place, so the product has one plus one, two decimal places.
<bookmark mark='point'/>Count two places from the right of one eight seven two.
The point goes after the eight, so we get eighteen point seven two.

narration: <bookmark mark='why'/>Step two, zero point one five six times zero point one two.
<bookmark mark='digits'/>The digits are again one hundred fifty six times twelve, which is one thousand eight hundred seventy two.
<bookmark mark='count'/>Zero point one five six has three decimal places, and zero point one two has two.
The product has three plus two, five decimal places.
<bookmark mark='point'/>The product has only four digits, so we write a zero in front to make five places.

narration: <bookmark mark='why'/>Step three, one hundred eighty seven point two divided by one point two.
<bookmark mark='ten'/>Multiply both numbers by ten, to get one thousand eight hundred seventy two divided by twelve.
<bookmark mark='fact'/>The fact says one hundred fifty six times twelve is one thousand eight hundred seventy two.
<bookmark mark='quot'/>The quotient is one hundred fifty six, because dividing undoes multiplying.
<bookmark mark='est1'/>Step four, estimate to check.
Fifteen times one point two is eighteen, so the first product is near eighteen.
<bookmark mark='est2'/>Zero point one five six is near zero point two.

<bookmark mark='ans'/>Fifteen point six times one point two is eighteen point seven two.
<bookmark mark='two'/>Zero point one five six times zero point one two is zero point zero one eight seven two.
<bookmark mark='quot'/>One hundred eighty seven point two divided by one point two is one hundred fifty six.

media.description: The digits two, four, five, eight and zero fill five boxes in a product of a number with one decimal place and another with one decimal place. The video places the digits to make the biggest product, the smallest product, one above one hundred fifty, one nearest one hundred and one nearest five.

media.teaching_notes: One idea: treat the product as whole numbers with two decimal places put back, then place the biggest digits where they add most to make a big product, and the smallest where they add least to make a small one. content.text:
Hidato
In Hidato, a grid of cells is given. It is usually square-shaped, like Sudoku or Kakuro, but it can also include hexagons or any shape that forms a tessellation. It can have inner holes (like a disc), but it is made of only one piece.
Usually, in every Hidato puzzle the lowest and the highest numbers are given on the grid.
Your task is to fill the grid such that there is a continuous path of consecutive numbers from the lowest to the highest number. The next number must be in any one of the adjacent cells, including diagonally adjacent cells.
The grid comes pre-filled with some numbers (with values between the smallest and the highest) to ensure that these puzzles have a single solution.
Try solving the following Hidato puzzles.
In each grid below, a number is a given cell, □ is a cell to fill and · is no cell.
Solved example (1 to 40), row 1: □ 33 35 □ □ · · ·
Solved example (1 to 40), row 2: □ □ 24 22 □ · · ·
Solved example (1 to 40), row 3: □ □ □ 21 □ □ · ·
Solved example (1 to 40), row 4: □ 26 □ 13 40 11 · ·

In Hidato, a grid of cells is given. It is usually square-shaped, like Sudoku or Kakuro, but it can also include hexagons or any shape that forms a tessellation. It can have inner holes (like a disc), but it is made of only one piece.

topics.summary: Multiplying decimals through fractions and decimal places, long division past the Ones, dividing by a decimal, divisions that never end, and leap years in one place.

content.text:
Summary
In this chapter, we learnt procedures to perform decimal multiplication and division.
For decimal multiplication, we first multiply the multiplier and multiplicand as counting numbers. The number of decimal digits in the product is the total number of decimal digits in the multiplier and multiplicand.
Division of decimals uses the same procedure, i.e., division using place value (long division), as with counting numbers. The regrouping continues after the Ones place to Tenths, Hundredths, Thousandths, and so on. When the Ones are regrouped to Tenths, a decimal point is placed in the quotient.
There are decimal divisions where the quotient never ends. After each regrouping and dividing there is always a remainder!

objectives.objective_text: Students name the tenth, hundredth and thousandth place of each digit of a decimal and write fractions with denominators 10, 100 and 1000 as decimals, including grams written in kilograms.
Students expand a fraction with denominator 10, 100, 1000 or 10000 as a sum of tenths, hundredths and thousandths, and divide any number by 10, 100 or 1000 by moving the decimal point left.
Students write fractions with denominators 10, 100 and 1000 as decimals and divide whole numbers by 10, 100 and 1000 by moving the decimal point.
Students find the cost of pens and the distance a car covers by writing each decimal as a fraction, multiplying, and converting the product back to a decimal.
Students test whether the product of two decimals, or of a decimal and a natural number, can be a natural number, and explain the answer with fractions.
Students convert metres to kilometres and multiply a decimal twice to find a weekly walking distance, and multiply two decimals to find the area of a rectangle.
Students multiply decimals in shopping, cloth, coin and profit problems by writing each decimal as a fraction, multiplying, and converting back, checking units before multiplying.
Students compare the digits after the decimal point in the multiplier, the multiplicand and the product for several products, and link the count to the zeroes in the denominator.
Students state the rule for multiplying decimals, use 596 × 248 = 147808 to write 5.96 × 24.8 at once, and find 5.8 × 1.24 by the rule and check it with fractions.
Students multiply decimals by the rule of decimal places, use a given whole-number product to write related decimal products, and multiply decimals by 10, 100 and 1000.
Students compute 2.25 × 8, 0.25 × 8 and 0.25 × 0.8 and compare each product with the two numbers multiplied.
Students sort products into three situations, both numbers greater than 1, both between 0 and 1, or one of each, and state how the product compares with the numbers in each.
Students predict whether a product is greater than both numbers, between them or less than both, and whether it is less than 1, before multiplying, then check.
Students find 3.9 ÷ 10 and 3.9 ÷ 100 by writing 3.9 as a fraction and multiplying by the reciprocal of the divisor, then write 0.039 m in centimetres and millimetres.
Students state the rule for dividing a decimal by 10, 100, 1000 and 10000, move the point left by the right number of places, and use it to complete a table.
Students divide decimals by 10, 100, 1000 and 10000 by moving the decimal point and convert lengths between metres, centimetres and millimetres.
Students share 29 m of ribbon between 2 and among 4 people by writing the share as a fraction and finding an equivalent fraction with denominator 10 or 100.
Students explain why 10/3 has no equivalent fraction with denominator 10, 100 or 1000, and why powers of 2 and 5 always give decimals that end.
Students write fractions as decimals by finding an equivalent fraction with denominator 10, 100 or 1000.
Students divide 1324 by 4 by long division, then divide 1325 by 4 and regroup the leftover Ones into Tenths and Hundredths, and verify with an equivalent fraction.
Students divide 237 by 8, regrouping Ones into Tenths, Tenths into Hundredths and Hundredths into Thousandths, and place the decimal point in the quotient.
Students divide a decimal dividend by a counting number by long division, placing the decimal point before dividing the Tenths and keeping zero place holders.
Students divide counting numbers and decimals by a counting number using equivalent fractions and long division, and choose the correct quotient from options.
Students find an average speed by dividing a distance by a decimal time, writing the divisor as a fraction and multiplying by its reciprocal.
Students find 4.68 ÷ 1.3 and 4.68 ÷ 0.13 by multiplying the dividend and the divisor by 10 or 100, and state the rule.
Students divide by decimals, use a given product to find related products and quotients, and fill in missing divisors and multipliers.
Students divide 10 by 3 by long division, notice the remainder 1 at every step, and find 10 ÷ 9 and 100 ÷ 11.
Students divide 1 by 7, list the remainders 1, 3, 2, 6, 4, 5 as a chain, and explain why the remainders and the quotient digits repeat in a cycle.
Students multiply 142857 by 1 to 7, notice the digits cycle round until 142857 × 7 = 999999, and recognise that 1 ÷ 17 gives another cyclic number and that Artin's question is still open.
Students run long divisions step by step, track the remainders, and decide whether each quotient ends or repeats, naming the repeating block.
Students compare 128 ÷ 4 with 128 ÷ 0.4, test other divisors, and make a table relating the dividend, the divisor and the quotient.
Students solve cutting, perimeter, sharing, petrol and flour problems by dividing decimals, predicting the size of each quotient first.
Students find how far the calendar falls behind the Earth after 100 years of 365 days by multiplying 0.2422 by 100.
Students count the days in 4 and in 100 calendar years with a leap day every 4th year, compare with 4 and 100 revolutions of the Earth, and see that the calendar overcompensates.
Students write the days in 100 and 1000 calendar years with no leap day in the 100th year, compare them with the Earth, and count the leap years in 1000 years under the 400th year rule.
Students count leap years and ordinary years under the full rule for a long span, compare the calendar with the Earth, and suggest a fix for the gap.
Students compare two packs of different weights by finding the price of 1 gram of each by decimal division.
Students solve price, number line, profit, shelf, unit and mixed fraction problems with decimal multiplication and division.
Students use one given whole-number product to write related decimal products and quotients by reasoning about decimal places and size.

Students use reasoning with decimal places to fill boxes for given products, use 756 ÷ 36 = 21 to find related quotients, complete a table of a ÷ b, arrange digits for target products, and order expressions by size.
Students restate the rule of decimal places for multiplication, the long division procedure that regroups past the Ones, how to divide by a decimal, and that some divisions never end.

chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's own order: multiplication first, then division, then the calendar story and a set of mixed problems. Every rule is reached from fractions the student already knows, so a decimal rule is never a trick to remember but a short cut for a fraction calculation.

points.text: The hook video leaves Arshad's pen bill open. The fraction method and the digit-counting rule arrive only after the student has tried to multiply a decimal on their own.
points.title: Try first, name later

points.text: A decimal is a fraction with denominator 10, 100 or 1000. Multiplying decimals multiplies those fractions, and dividing by a decimal multiplies by its reciprocal, so both rules are explained rather than told.
points.title: Fractions underneath every rule

points.text: Long division regroups Ones into Tenths, Tenths into Hundredths and so on. The decimal point in the quotient appears at the moment Ones are regrouped into Tenths.
points.title: Place value carries division past the Ones

points.text: Each idea gets its own topic with one video per concept and a practice concept at the end; interactive tools appear only where handling the numbers is the idea. The book's questions follow in their own topic, one question and one video per concept.
points.title: Concept, then practice, topic by topic
